citations.claim: These sources were written for work where a mistake kills people and can't be undone: the Marine Corps doctrine manual *Warfighting* (MCDP 1), the Columbia Accident Investigation Board report, the US
The OpenStax *Principles of Management* text says vague, direction-only planning ("domain planning") belongs at the top of an organisation, where uncertainty is high.
Precise goal-setting, it says, belongs in "the technical core, where there is less uncertainty."
Cascading measurable targets from the top down to everyone goes further than the textbook does.
The textbook's case for specific targets is real: "Research suggests that goal planning results in higher levels of performance than does domain planning alone."
*Warfighting* builds the hierarchy around something else.
Every order has two parts: "The task describes the action to be taken while the intent describes the purpose of the action."
The purpose takes priority, because events can make a task pointless while the purpose still holds.
Subordinates should understand the purpose of the commander two levels above them.
And "the senior prescribes the method of execution only to the degree that is essential for coordination."
The manual even warns that good information technology "can tempt us to try to maintain precise, positive control over subordinates."
The Columbia board found that the shuttle programme did not fail through one bad decision.
Foam kept breaking off the fuel tank on launch, and each flight that came back safely made it look acceptable: "With no engineering analysis, Shuttle managers used past success as a justification for
"Taken one at a time, each decision seemed correct."
The board found that there was real pressure to hold a launch date, and that "The Program was operating too close to too many margins."
The nuclear handbook makes the measurement point directly: "things are counted because they can be," and results are lagging indicators that don't show whether performance will continue.
The Army manual bans grading in reviews: "Chart after chart of ratios, bar graphs, and tables quickly obscures any meaning."
The board's fix is to move the burden of proof: "operations must be proved safe, rather than the other way around."
Its example question is "Prove to me that Columbia has not been harmed."
The nuclear handbook says "A just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture."
It also says "The organization is perfectly tuned to get the performance it receives from the workforce."
The wildfire guide is blunter: "Information is the lifeblood of safety."
It asks whether learning should depend on luck: "Should a chance occurrence of two inches be the determining factor for organizational learning?" (A falling tree missed a firefighter by that much.)
The NHS Just Culture guide starts from the view that "Action singling out an individual is rarely appropriate."
The textbook's expectancy theory says the opposite: pay and reward should depend on results.
Judging by results is what these sources call outcome bias.
To be fair, the textbook already argues against punishment as a main tool and against forced ranking.
The Columbia board found that information was condensed and simplified as it rose through management.
It warned that fixing only the broken part or the nearest person creates a "belief that the underlying problem has been solved."
It noted that NASA's post-Challenger reforms had faded by the time of Columbia.
And: "NASA's blind spot is it believes it has a strong safety culture."
The wildfire guide adds two warnings: Leaders who receive a review tend to jump to the recommendations, write an action plan, and believe the problem is solved.
Recommendations often "add complexity to the workplace, which has the paradoxical effect of increasing risk."
It also found that reviews rarely examine the decisions of the senior official who ordered them.
The textbook itself says top-down change "rely[s] on mechanistic assumptions about the nature of an organization."
The Columbia board's version: "Leaders create culture. It is their responsibility to change it."
*Warfighting* wants "no 'zero defects' mentality."
It deals gently with errors of overboldness and harshly with inaction.
The nuclear handbook aims for zero significant events and tells workers to pause when unsure.
It wants conservative decisions that put safety ahead of near-term production.
The Army manual makes retraining routine: soldiers must understand "they did not perform the task to standard."
The nuclear handbook calls retraining people for automatic slips "a waste of time and is an insult to the worker."
The wildfire guide lists "forced retraining" among the disciplinary actions it promises not to take.
The nuclear handbook runs root-cause analysis.
The Columbia board issued recommendations and new independent authorities.
The wildfire guide says its reviews "must avoid causal statements," and only issues recommendations through a separate, vetted process.
The NHS and nuclear guides use step-by-step tests to decide when one person is at fault.
The wildfire guide sets the bar at reckless and wilful disregard.
*Warfighting* tolerates honest error but says people who simply agree with the boss to get ahead ("yes-men") will not be tolerated.
The Columbia board left personal accountability to a separate process from its investigation.
The wildfire guide's reluctance to make recommendations may be impractical when you need a decision by Friday.
The textbook's planning-to-returns evidence is thin (it says so itself), but so is the evidence against it for firms like yours.

ideas.idea: Commander's intent and mission tactics: state the task and its purpose, prescribe method only as far as coordination needs, against cascading KPIs that prescribe outputs
Subordinates should understand intent two levels up
Friction and uncertainty are the normal condition; plans that assume otherwise deny the nature of the work
No zero-defects mentality: be lenient on bold errors and severe on inaction, against appraisal systems that punish visible mistakes
Deference to expertise and a reluctance to simplify: decisions migrate to whoever knows most, not to rank
Preoccupation with failure: treat weak signals and near-misses as data, against dashboards that report green
Normalization of deviance and schedule pressure: a success record is not evidence of safety; Columbia's foam
An independent technical authority or safety function with its own line, not one that reports to the programme it checks
Work as imagined versus work as done; learn why the action made sense at the time, not who broke the rule
The after-action review: leaders enter the discussion only when necessary, it is permissible to disagree, no critique or lecture
What the textbooks teach that the doctrine contradicts: management by objectives and goal cascades; control systems; change managed through a programme
A disagreement among the doctrine sources: the war-fighting doctrine prizes tempo, boldness and accepting risk; the high-reliability sources prize redundancy, verification and stopping when unsure
Simple, complicated, complex: the playbook fits the complicated case and fails in the complex one

note: Accurate and well-sourced; every listed quotation found except one with a marked [s] alteration (graded no by rule; otherwise verbatim). The one none: 'cascading goes further than the textbook' is contradicted by the textbook's own cascade and MBO passages; 'domain planning belongs at the top' turns the textbook's descriptive 'likely to prevail' into a prescription. The sources never use 'outcome bias' (the wildfire guide says hindsight bias). Missing: friction, deference to expertise, work-as-done credited to a source.
